title: Monitoring and troubleshooting
summary: Cluster Manager metrics and the Prometheus endpoint, alert types and thresholds, cluster and server logs, the job scheduler, support package generation and contents, and failure playbooks for node down, endpoint unreachable, license/cert expiry, and memory pressure.

blocks.body:
Monitoring Redis Software is three surfaces plus a feedback loop: metrics and alerts (the numbers and the push notifications), logs (the story of what happened), and the job scheduler (the recurring machinery) — with the support package as the artifact you hand Redis support when the loop fails. `rladmin status` remains the fastest text-mode health check, expecting `OK` for cluster, nodes, endpoints, and shards.

## Metrics and the Prometheus endpoint

The Cluster Manager UI charts metrics per cluster, node, database, and shard; the REST API exposes the same numbers. The **metrics stream engine** is the modern export path — generally available in Redis Software 8.0, it exposes a v2 Prometheus scraping endpoint at `https://<cluster_name>:8070/v2`, streams all time-series metrics to external tools, and enables real-time monitoring (v1 monitoring — UI and REST — remains for older setups). `rladmin metrics` configures the cluster-wide metrics stream engine from the CLI. Off-cluster, Redis publishes integration guides for Grafana, Datadog, Dynatrace, and New Relic. Watch license quotas as metrics too: `cluster_shards_limit` shows the shard limit by shard type (RAM or flash) and `bdb_shards_used` shows shards used per database — the numbers that tell you before a provisioning failure that you are near the license ceiling.

## Alerts: types and thresholds

Alerts are threshold-based and configured in the UI (Cluster > Configuration > Alerts Settings) or the REST API (`alert_settings`). They fall in familiar buckets: cluster alerts such as license expiry (the `cluster_license_about_to_expire` alert fires by default 7 days before expiration, threshold configurable — 30 days is a sensible value), database alerts configurable per database with their own thresholds, and node/resource alerts — the docs' sizing guidance tells you where the alert-level lines sit: one node above 65% RAM is a migrate-something signal, all nodes above 70% is a scale-out signal, and nodes above 80% CPU mean move shards or scale out. One special-case threshold worth memorizing: an Active-Active database starts evicting at 80% of its memory limit.

## Logs

Two vantage points: the UI **Cluster > Logs** screen (system and user events: alerts, notifications, configuration actions, who did what, when, and whether it succeeded) and the server filesystem — logs live by default in `/var/opt/redislabs/log/`, with `event_log.log` the first file to open for cluster events. The Redis slow log has an operator-side view for latency work, and rsyslog forwarding is supported for shipping events off-node. Log rotation is not your concern — the cluster's job scheduler runs logrotate every five minutes.

## The job scheduler

The cluster runs a job scheduler for recurring maintenance: log rotation (logrotate every five minutes), certificate rotation, CCS rotation, and Redis cleanup jobs, configured through the job scheduler REST API (`/v1/job_scheduler`). Practical consequence: certificate rotation and log management are scheduled machinery, so an operator's job is to verify the jobs are healthy rather than hand-roll cron replacements.

## Support packages

When the loop fails and you escalate, the support package is the artifact: a zip archive (downloaded as `debuginfo.tar.gz` from the UI) containing all cluster configuration and logs — per-database directories with CCS info, client lists, `INFO` output, rladmin-style database info (memory limit, persistence type, eviction policy, hashing policy), and slowlog data (included only when `slowlog_in_sanitized_support` is enabled), plus per-node directories with configs, logs, rladmin status output, Envoy config, and system information (processes, disk usage, memory, network interfaces). Generate it from the UI (**Support** > Generate, scoped full, per-database, or per-node) or from the CLI: `rladmin cluster debug_info` (per-node fallback: `/opt/redislabs/bin/debuginfo`), and via REST with `GET /v1/cluster/debuginfo`. It takes several minutes and loads the system; if it fails for lack of /tmp space, move the save path with `rladmin cluster config debuginfo_path <path>`.

## Playbooks

**Node down.** Confirm from `rladmin status` and the UI. The cluster heals automatically — a replica is promoted — so the operator's job is verification and replacement: check nodes, endpoints, and shards all report OK after failover; if the host is gone, remove the node and add a replacement (or rejoin with `replace_node` to reuse the ID); run `rlcheck` on surviving nodes afterwards. For planned work, `rladmin node <id> maintenance_mode on` migrates shards away first, and `off` before anything considers the node normal again.

**Database endpoint unreachable.** Work the path from client to shard: confirm the endpoint with `rladmin status` (endpoints section) and try `redis-cli` (in `/opt/redislabs/bin`) from a node. If the endpoint works by IP but not FQDN, DNS is the culprit. Check the port (10000-19999) is open through firewalls, and check the endpoint's proxy placement policy (`rladmin bind`). Clients that cannot resolve the FQDN can use the discovery service on port 8001 (Sentinel-compatible) to look the endpoint up by database name.

**License or certificate expiry.** Both are calendar failures you can see coming. License: the expiry alert (default 7 days) gives lead time; expiry blocks database configuration changes and new databases but keeps serving — apply the renewed key in Cluster > Configuration > General > License and nothing is lost. Certificates: the job scheduler rotates them, but CA-signed replacements are your procurement; replace them through the certificates REST API/UI before expiry, because an expired UI (`cm`) or proxy (`proxy`) cert is a self-inflicted outage.

**High memory and eviction.** Node level: above 65% RAM on one node, migrate shards (`rladmin migrate`) to cooler nodes; above 70% on all nodes, add a node; keep ~30% free for buffers. Database level: check the memory limit and eviction policy, and whether size is approaching the limit (the UI per-database metrics and `bdb_shards_used`-style quota metrics); an approaching Active-Active database evicts at 80% of its memory limit. Persistent and ephemeral storage alerts belong to the same family — full disks break backups and persistence, not just capacity.

## Exam takeaways

- The v2 Prometheus endpoint is `https://<cluster_name>:8070/v2` (metrics stream engine, GA in Redis Software 8.0); Grafana/Datadog integrations consume it; `cluster_shards_limit` and `bdb_shards_used` expose license quotas.
- Alerts are threshold-based with UI and REST configuration; license-expiry default is 7 days before expiration; sizing thresholds — 65% RAM per node, 70% cluster-wide, 80% CPU — are the operator's tripwires; Active-Active eviction starts at 80% of the memory limit.
- Logs: UI under Cluster > Logs, files under `/var/opt/redislabs/log/` (start with `event_log.log`); the job scheduler runs logrotate every five minutes, plus certificate rotation, CCS rotation, and cleanup jobs via `/v1/job_scheduler`.
- Support package = `debuginfo.tar.gz` via Support screen, `rladmin cluster debug_info`, or `GET /v1/cluster/debuginfo`; it bundles configs, logs, status output, slowlog (opt-in), and per-node system info.
- Playbooks: node down → verify failover, replace, `rlcheck`; endpoint unreachable → IP-vs-FQDN isolates DNS, check ports and `rladmin bind` policy; license/cert expiry → alerts give lead time, renewal is non-disruptive; memory pressure → migrate or scale out before eviction.
